clue.text: Singer in clubs given a wave

blocks.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
taken as written
a roller is a long heavy wave breaking on the shore

explanation.surface: A vocalist performing at nightclubs gets a friendly wave from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests nightclubs, but it is the card suit; the pieces simply follow one another to make CAROLLER.
explanation.definitionFit: A caroller is someone who sings carols, typically going door to door at Christmas, so is a kind of vocalist.

clue.text: Stole bags obtained in Hispanic capital

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it and hold it inside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a boa is a long feathery scarf or stole
got means obtained

explanation.surface: A thief pockets loot in a Spanish-speaking city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' reads as the past tense of steal, but it is the noun, a scarf worn round the shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: Bogotá is the capital city of Colombia, a Spanish-speaking country in South America.

clue.text: Unfussy consumers of old French wine upset going through customs

indicators.note: in a down clue, something upset is turned upside down, so its letters run the other way
passing through something means being inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
vin is the French word for wine
mores are the customs and conventions of a society

explanation.surface: Easy-going drinkers knock back old French wine while passing through customs at the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customs' suggests a border checkpoint, but here it means social conventions. The upturned wine goes in after the first letter of the customs word.
explanation.definitionFit: Omnivores eat both plant and animal food, so they are literally unfussy eaters, a playful description.

clue.text: With drinks I notice flavouring of absinthe

indicators.note: whatever is drunk ends up inside the drinker, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: and means with, in addition to
to notice is to see, so 'I notice' is I SEE

explanation.surface: Someone sipping drinks picks up the taste of absinthe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinks' looks like the noun for beverages, but it is a verb: the word for 'with' swallows I SEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aniseed is the liquorice-tasting seed of the anise plant, the dominant taste in absinthe and similar spirits.

clue.text: Liverpool fan, say, put up times for crucial match

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up raises it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Liverpool FC play in red and their supporters are called Reds; 'say' marks an example
by means times in multiplication, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A football supporter posts kick-off times for a big game.
explanation.walkthrough: Liverpool FC is an English football club whose fans are nicknamed the Reds. 'Say' tells you the fan is one example of a Red.
explanation.definitionFit: A derby is a match between local rivals, often seen as the most important fixture of the season.

clue.text: Amounts of data from alumnus, one clad in skirts

indicators.note: being clad in clothing means being wrapped inside it, so the garments enclose the rest

blocks.note: OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a school
I is the Roman numeral one
kilts are pleated Scottish skirts

explanation.surface: Some statistic is gathered from a former student dressed in a kilt.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy (OB) is the British term for a former pupil of a school; with one he goes inside the Scottish garments.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilobit is a unit of digital information of a thousand bits, so the plural means quantities of data.

clue.text: Attend university party, initially the worse for wear

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: to attend an event is to be at it
U is the standard abbreviation for university
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A student goes to a university party and ends up looking a bit rough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attend' wants to be a single word for going, but to attend something is simply to be present there.
explanation.definitionFit: A beat-up car or coat is battered and shabby from use, which is what looking rough and worn means.

clue.text: Dip bagel in starchy food

blocks.note: to sag is to dip or droop downward
a bagel is ring-shaped, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone dunks a bagel into a bowl of something starchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dip' looks like dunking, but it means a sag; the bagel stands for O by its round shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Sago is a starch taken from palm pith, used in puddings, so it is a carbohydrate foodstuff.

clue.text: Move on tide at sea in Atlantic port

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship sails out on the tide from a harbour on the Atlantic coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The nautical picture makes 'at sea' read literally, but it signals that the first three words are scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay, lies on the River Plate estuary opening onto the Atlantic, and is a major harbour city.

clue.text: Shakespeare role, sweet one, seized by returning star

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so its letters run backwards
whatever is seized is held in a grip, so it sits inside the other piece

blocks.note: a Polo is a British brand of ring-shaped mint sweet
I is the Roman numeral one
the sun is a star

explanation.surface: An actor in a Shakespeare play, a sweet one, is grabbed by a star making a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: The sweet is a Polo mint, the British sweet with a hole; 'star' suggests a celebrity, but it is our own sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius is the meddling old courtier in Hamlet, father of Ophelia and Laertes, so he is a part in a play.

clue.text: Bewail gutless German chap getting under the table

indicators.note: without guts means with the insides removed, so only the outermost letters remain

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
Otto is a common German man's name

explanation.surface: A cowardly German man laments as he ends up under the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutless' reads as cowardly, but it means the word loses its middle. BLOTTO is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Being under the table is an idiom for having drunk so much you collapse, and blotto is slang for extremely drunk.

clue.text: Car lover follows motorists round cliff, occasionally

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is taken
to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
to follow is to come after, so this piece is placed behind the rest

blocks.note: the AA, the Automobile Association, is a British motorists' organisation
the second and fourth letters of the word
Romeo, from Shakespeare, is the archetypal lover

explanation.surface: A petrolhead trails some drivers around a clifftop road now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA is the Automobile Association, Britain's big motoring breakdown club. 'Car lover' reads as one phrase, but the car is the definition and the lover is a wordplay piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfa Romeo is an Italian manufacturer of sporty automobiles, so one of its models is an example of a motor vehicle.

clue.text: Thin and delicate current agent put on weight

indicators.note: in an across clue, placing something on another sets it after that piece

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for weight
I is the symbol for electric current
a spy is a secret agent

explanation.surface: A once-slim secret agent has piled on the pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on weight' reads as gaining pounds, but it means the current-plus-agent pieces sit after the weight letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Wispy describes something fine, slight and insubstantial, like a wisp of hair or smoke.

clue.text: Criminal circle had system for dealing with issue

indicators.note: criminal means crooked and bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gang of crooks had a scheme for handling a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' suggests a problem to deal with, but it is the formal word for offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is an old legal term for offspring, so arrangements for looking after children fit the description.

clue.text: Crew that’s second-class getting teased

blocks.note: B grade is second class
to rag someone is to tease them, so being teased is getting ragged

explanation.surface: A second-rate team of rowers or sailors is mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' looks like a team, but it is the past tense of crow, to boast. To rag is British for teasing.
explanation.definitionFit: Crew is an old past tense of crow, to boast loudly, so it means boasted or showed off.

clue.text: Chatterbox’s viable plan to ingest second drink

indicators.note: to ingest is to take inside the body, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a goer is an idea or scheme likely to succeed
S is the abbreviation for second
a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: A talker's workable scheme involves having another drink.
explanation.walkthrough: ''s' here is 'is', joining definition to wordplay. A goer is British informal for a plan that will work.
explanation.definitionFit: A gossiper chats idly about other people's affairs, so is a talkative person who can't stop nattering.

clue.text: Make musicartist from America run off

indicators.note: off means taken away, so a letter is dropped from the longer word

blocks.note: the surname of James McNeill, the Massachusetts-born painter known for a portrait of his mother
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: An American musician makes a getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run off' reads as fleeing, but it means the R comes off WHISTLER, the American painter famous for his portrait of his mother. The printed clue runs 'music' and 'artist' together.
explanation.definitionFit: Whistling through pursed lips produces a tune, so it is a simple way of playing melody without an instrument.

clue.text: Hide from essayist’s family

blocks.note: Charles Lamb was an English essayist, so this is Lamb's
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: Someone hides away from a writer's relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for an animal skin. Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambskin is the skin of a young sheep, often with the wool on, so it is a type of animal pelt.

clue.text: Delays criminal activities

blocks.note: first meaning: hindrances that slow things down, like traffic jams
second meaning: armed robberies

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a verb, delaying crimes, but both halves are plural nouns naming the same word in two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Hold-ups are both stoppages that slow progress and robberies at gunpoint, two everyday senses of the compound noun.

clue.text: Snappy leader of business venture

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to venture something is to risk it, and a venture is a risk

explanation.surface: A short-tempered boss heads up a commercial enterprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snappy leader' reads as a curt boss, but 'Snappy' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy can mean quick and lively, as in a snappy pace, which is what brisk means.

clue.text: Ethnic American spies infiltrating opposing sides

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside an organisation, so one piece slips into another

blocks.note: right and left are opposite sides
A is the abbreviation for American
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: American secret agents work their way into both camps of a conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opposing sides' sounds like warring factions, but it means the letters for right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic and racial are close synonyms, both relating to groups of people sharing descent or culture.

clue.text: E.g. Othello, in vessel going west, potters here?

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another
in an across clue, heading west means travelling right to left, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice
a sloop is a type of sailing boat

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Moor sails west, while craftsmen make pots somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The Moor goes in after the first letter of the boat, then the whole lot runs backwards. 'Potters' are not ceramicists but players potting balls.
explanation.definitionFit: Players of pool or snooker pot balls, so rooms with pool tables are where such potting goes on; the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Works from Engels are potentially revolutionary

indicators.note: taking something from a stretch of text means lifting a run of letters straight out of it
a revolution is a turning round, so the extracted run is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: The writings of Friedrich Engels, Marx's collaborator, might stir up a revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: Engels and 'revolutionary' paint a Marxist picture, but the works are musical, not political, and 'revolutionary' only turns the letters round: read SAREPO backwards to get OPERAS.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a staged musical drama, and 'work' is the standard term for a composer's individual composition.

clue.text: Number six minus nine, divisible by two?

indicators.note: minus means take away, so some letters are removed from the word before it

blocks.note: taken as written
IX is the Roman numeral nine
an even number divides exactly by two

explanation.surface: A puzzling sum: six take away nine, and is the result even?
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as arithmetic, but the subtraction is of letters: the Roman nine is struck from the word six. The question mark admits the answer itself is odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven is an integer, the one after six, so it fits the plain description of a figure.

clue.text: Journalist’s copy probing case of sabotage?

indicators.note: a case is the outside casing, so only the outermost letters are used
a probe pokes inside something, so one piece pushes into another

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
to crib is to copy someone else's work

explanation.surface: A reporter's article investigates an apparent act of sabotage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copy' looks like a journalist's text, but it is a verb meaning to crib; ''s' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scribe is a jocular or informal term for a writer, especially a newspaper hack.

clue.text: Mussolini pinching that man’s small table cover

indicators.note: to pinch something is to squeeze it between two parts, so the outer piece grips the rest

blocks.note: Il Duce, the leader, was Mussolini's title
that man is 'he', and 'he's' contracts 'he is'
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: The Italian dictator steals a man's little tablecloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' reads as stealing, but it means squeezing the other pieces in. 'Small' looks like it describes the table, but it is just a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A duchesse is an embroidered cloth or set of mats laid on a dressing table, an antique furnishing term.

clue.text: Look around with queen, following willing worker on estate (or any across answer here?)

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
following means coming after, so these pieces are placed behind the next one

blocks.note: to be game is to be willing to try something
a peek is a quick look
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's monogram

explanation.surface: A servant on a country estate glances around while a queen is about.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is a puzzle-wide joke: every across answer hides a game (SAGO has GO, BLOTTO has LOTTO, WHISTLE has WHIST), so each keeps one. A gamekeeper looks after game birds on a British country estate.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper is employed on a private landholding to rear and protect game birds and animals for shooting.

clue.text: Glaswegian’s opposed to single drink

blocks.note: a means one, single
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A Glaswegian refuses a solo tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glaswegian's' tells you the definition is a Scots dialect form; Glasgow is Scotland's largest city.
explanation.definitionFit: Agin is a Scots and dialect word for against, which is what opposed to means when used as a preposition.
